entries.title: India news: IndiGo engine failure triggers airport emergency
entries.summary: Chennai airport declared full emergency after an IndiGo flight suffered an engine failure, hours after reports that an Air India pilot involved in an on-air incident last week tested positive in a drug test. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India news: IndiGo engine failure triggers airport emergency

Published August 12, 2026last updated August 12, 2026

Chennai airport declared full emergency after an IndiGo flight suffered an engine failure, hours after reports that an Air India pilot involved in an on-air incident last week tested positive in a drug test. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Chennai airport declared a full emergency after an IndiGo flight suffered an engine failure
  • The pilot of an Air India flight that suddenly lost altitude last week tested positive for marijuana

Here's a roundup of the biggest headlines from India on Wednesday, August 12:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Air India pilot tests positive in drug test

Air India pilot tests positive in drug test

The captain of an Air India flight from Phuket to Delhi that suddenly lost altitude last week tested positive for marijuana in a confirmatory drug test.

The Airbus A320neo, carrying 137 passengers and eight crew, lost about 300 feet of over Odisha before landing safely in Delhi.

The plane stabilized and landed safely. India's Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau has classified the incident as serious.

The incident had left 13 passengers and four crew members injured, and led to India's aviation ministry summoning Air India CEO Campbell Wilson on Tuesday.

Skip next section Emergency at Chennai airport after IndiGo plane suffers engine failure

Emergency at Chennai airport after IndiGo plane suffers engine failure

Late on Tuesday night, Chennai airport declared a full emergency after an IndiGo flight suffered an engine failure, media reports said.

This came only a few hours after reports emerged that the captain of an Air India flight that suddenly lost altitude last week, injuring crew and passengers, tested positive in a drug test, further plunging India's aviation into turmoil.

On Tuesday, the pilot of an IndiGo plane, flying from Kolkata to Chennai with 224 people on board, noticed that the left engine had failed while the plane prepared to land, reports said Airports Authority of India (AAI) officials.

Airport authorities activated emergency response measures, which remained in place till the plane landed safely. The declaration of full emergency was withdrawn soon after.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi Studio bringing you the latest updates from across India.

The turbulence in Indian aviation continues, as Chennai airport declared a full emergency on Tuesday after an IndiGo flight suffered an engine failure. This comes on the heels of reports that the captain of an Air India flight that suddenly lost altitude last week, injuring crew and passengers, has tested positive in a drug test. 

Meanwhile, quick-commerce firms Zepto and Blinkit are under the scanner over "serious food safety and hygiene violations." Your deliveries may still arrive within minutes, but in what condition? That's the question.

For all this and more, stay tuned to our blog.

entries.title: Pakistan says 3 nationals killed in Houthi Red Sea attack
entries.summary: Pakistan's foreign minister has said Islamabad "strongly condemns" Houthi attacks on commercial vessels while offering condolences to the families of the dead.
entries.content:
Pakistan

Pakistan says 3 nationals killed in Houthi Red Sea attack

August 12, 2026

Pakistan's foreign minister has said Islamabad "strongly condemns" Houthi attacks on commercial vessels while offering condolences to the families of the dead.

At least three Pakistani nations were killed in an "incident involving an attack on a commercial vessel in the Red Sea," Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on Wednesday. 

Another Pakistani national had sustained injuries.

"Pakistan strongly condemns the Houthi attack on a non-combatant commercial vessel. Such attacks endanger innocent lives, constitute a violation of international law, and pose a serious threat to freedom of navigation, maritime security, and the safety of commercial shipping in the Red Sea," the minister said in a post on X. 

Pakistan's Foreign Ministry was in contact with Saudi Arabia and Yemen to ascertain further details of the incident, Dar said. Meanwhile, the Pakistani Embassy in Riyadh was coordinating the retrieval and repatriation of the mortal remains of their deceased nationals.

Vessels under attack amid Middle East conflict

On Tuesday, the US and Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels reported separate attacks on shipping as peace negotiations between Washington and Tehran seemingly stagnated once again.

At the southern end of the Red Sea, a suspected Houthi attack on a small cargo vessel killed four crew members, Yemen's Transport Ministry said. It was not immediately clear is this was the same vessel Dar was referring to.

Commercial shipping and seafarers passing through the Middle East have increasingly come under attack by both the US and Iran since the conflict began earlier this year. 

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: Australia approves new rules benefiting gig delivery workers
entries.summary: Delivery drivers in Australia are to be guaranteed "world-leading" higher pay and insurance cover on the job. The move could be a model for other countries.
entries.content:
August 12, 2026

Delivery drivers in Australia are to be guaranteed "world-leading" higher pay and insurance cover on the job. The move could be a model for other countries.

Food and grocery delivery workers in Australia will be paid at least A$31.30 (€19.15, $22.11) an hour and be given accident insurance on the job under new rules approved by Australia's industrial relations tribunal.

The hourly rate, set out in an order issued by the Fair Work Commission (FWC) on Tuesday, is above Australia's minimum wage of A$26.44.

The FWC's order, which could serve as a precedent for other countries, has been hailed by the Transport Workers Union (TWU) as "a landmark moment for the Australian gig economy." The union called the new rules a "world-leading set of standards."

What rights and protects did the FWC give gig delivery drivers?

The minimum hourly rate will be paid for "engaged" time, i.e. the time between taking on a delivery job and completing the commission.

The order, which takes effect on August 17, also requires companies to provide a "reasonable minimum level of cover" ​for personal accident insurance on the job, without specifying exactly how much.

The workers will, however, still be responsible for maintaining ⁠third-party ⁠insurance for the vehicles used for deliveries.

Unions and workers in Australia ​have long sought ⁠reforms benefiting gig workers.

They have previously not been covered by many of the protections given to other employees, being classified as "independent contractors."

The new rules are expected to affect some 250,000 workers.

UN moves to protect gig workers

The FWC's order comes after the United Nations' International Labour Organization (ILO) in June adopted a new global treaty for decent working conditions in the gig economy.

The standards laid down in the treaty, the first global treaty of its kind, still need ratification by governments.

In Australia, the parliament passed legislation in 2023 and 2024 under the center-left Labor government that granted gig workers more negotiating rights over minimum pay and working conditions.

Those laws gave the FWC the power to set rules for pay and insurance.

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: Indonesia: Passengers rescued after Bali ferry catches fire
entries.summary: Authorities said they had visually confirmed that no passengers remained on the burning ferry, but were still confirming the total number.
entries.content:
Indonesia

Indonesia: Passengers rescued after Bali ferry catches fire

August 12, 2026

Authorities said they had visually confirmed that no passengers remained on the burning ferry, but were still confirming the total number.

Indonesian authorities rescued over 130 people from a burning ferry on Wednesday near the tourist island of Bali.

The fire broke out on the Padang Bai-Lembar ferry route connecting Bali and Lombok and is also used by tourists travelling between the two popular destinations.

It is the second major ferry fire in Indonesia this month.

What Indonesian authorities said about the ferry fire

Muhammad Hariyadi, who heads the Mataram Search and Rescue Office, told Metro TV that all passengers had been rescued and there were no immediate reports of casualties.

"We have approached the ship and confirmed that all passengers are no longer on board," he said. "We visually see no passengers on the ship."

In a statement later, Hariyadi said the total number of passengers on board was still being verified. He had initially said the ferry was carrying 114 passengers and 17 crew members, referring to the passenger manifest data released by Padang Bai's port authority.

The ferry also had 44 vehicles and 53 motorcycles on it.

What else do we know about the fire and rescue efforts?

Fire broke out on board the Putri Yasmin Ferry at about 4:15 a.m. (1045 GMT) while it was en route from Padang Bai port in Bali to Lembar port on the adjacent island of Lombok, according to the search office in Mataram.

The agency received an emergency report nearly half an hour later and then deployed rescue vessels and personnel.

The burning ferry was in the midst of rough seas with waves as high as 4 meters (13 feet), Hariyadi said, adding that conditions had complicated rescue efforts.

A ferry in the vicinity had evacuated 30 passengers and brought them to Bali. A search and rescue vessel was on its way to Lembar port with 59 of the rescued passengers. A naval vessel picked up another 17 passengers.

Marine safety in Indonesia

Marine accidents are a regular occurrence in Indonesia where ferries are a common mode of transport.

Last week, five people died in a ferry fire off the coast of Java Island. Last month, a ferry transporting more than 70 people sank while sailing near Seayar Island. The rescue operation had been closed after four bodies were recovered, but 14 were officially still missing.

And in July last year, a ferry sank while travelling between Java and Bali, killing nearly 20 people.

Edited by: Rob Turner

entries.title: North Korea tests missile ahead of US-South Korea drills
entries.summary: The suspected ballistic missile was launched towards Japan and likely fell just outside of its special economic zone, Tokyo said.
entries.content:
North Korea

North Korea tests missile ahead of US-South Korea drills

August 12, 2026

The suspected ballistic missile was launched towards Japan and likely fell just outside of its special economic zone, Tokyo said.

North Korea test-fired a ballistic missile off its east coast towards Japan early on Wednesday, its neighbors said, just days before US-South Korea Joint Military drills which Pyongyang views as invasion rehearsals.

This is the second such test in less than a week.

"Our military detected at around 6:00 am (2100 GMT on Tuesday) a ballistic missile launched by North Korea from the Wonsan area towards the East Sea," Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a message to reporters.

Japan's Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi called the launch a "threat to peace and security in our region," adding that Tokyo had lodged a strong protest with North Korea through diplomatic channels in Beijing.

"It's a serious problem that affects the safety of the Japanese people," he said at a press conference.

Here's what we know about North Korea's test-launch from Japan:

  • North Korea launched at least one ballistic missile on Wednesday morning
  • Details were under close joint analysis between Japan, the US and South Korea
  • Missile estimated to have fallen outside Japan's exclusive economic zone in the Sea of Japan
  • Japan's prime minister issued instructions to maintain a complete state of readiness
  • No reports of damage have been confirmed

North's message ahead of joint military drills

The suspected ballistic missile launch came just two days after South Korea and the US announced that they will kick off their annual joint military drills on August 17.

The upcoming drills are a regular summer feature, designed to coordinate their defense against the nuclear-armed Pyongyang.

North Korea has condemned these drills on several occasions before, often staging missile tests before and after the exercises.

"North Korea has never simply let a South Korea-US joint military exercise pass without a response," said Lim Eul-chul, a North Korea expert at Kyungnam University.

"This is a message that Pyongyang is closely watching the upcoming drills and could stage a provocation if it deems one necessary," he said.

After last year's drills began, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un claimed the exercise had grown more provocative than before and showed Seoul and Washington's "will to ignite a war." He said it had prompted North Korea to respond with “proactive and overwhelming” countermeasures.

On August 6, the US, South Korea and Japan detected the launch of a short-range ballistic missile from the North in what was its first ballistic weapons testing activity since late June.

Pyongyang, which ususally releases details of tests a day later, did not initially confirm the launch.

entries.title: Drone attack hits Libya's largest oil refinery
entries.summary: Fires broke out at the Zawiya oil complex after explosives-laden drones struck the site. Hours later, fresh violence in Benghazi highlighted Libya's persistent security challenges.
entries.content:
Libya

Drone attack hits Libya's largest oil refinery

August 12, 2026

Fires broke out at the Zawiya oil complex after explosives-laden drones struck the site. Hours later, fresh violence in Benghazi highlighted Libya's persistent security challenges.

Libya's National Oil Corporation (NOC) said Tuesday that fires at a fuel storage facility had been quickly brought under control after a drone attack.

The Zawiya oil complex west of Tripoli is home to the country's largest refinery and has been the scene of repeated armed clashes between warring factions fighting for primacy in the country since the fall of former strongman leader Moammar Gadhafi in 2011.

What happened in the drone attack on Libya's Zawiya oil refinery?

Monday's attack by an as yet undeclared actor targeted the Zawiya Oil Refining Company with explosives-laden drones, causing a tank containing about 4.5 million liters (1.2 million gallons) of gasoline to collapse after a fire.

Owner Brega Petroleum Marketing said the fires had been brought under control far faster than expected, with engineers telling Reuters news agency that damage had been limited, though operations were interrupted.

In a statement on X, Abdulhamid Dbeibah, Libya's internationally recognized prime minister, wrote that the crime of targeting civilian infrastructure would "not go unanswered."

"The use of drones to strike vital facilities," wrote Dbeibah, "is not a random incident, but rather an organized and dangerous act that requires a firm response to protect the state and its institutions and prevent its recurrence."

Officials from Libya's electricity provider said two further drones targeted the Zawiya power plant early Tuesday morning, with one hitting the fire-fighting system but causing no damage.

What is the security situation in divided Libya?

Libya has remained divided since the 2011 uprising that toppled Gadhafi. Dbeibah's UN-recognized government is based in Tripoli in the west, while eastern and parts of southern Libya are controlled by the Libyan National Army (LNA), a military force led by commander Khalifa Haftar.

Amid those tensions, the LNA said its head of military intelligence, Fawzi al-Mansouri, was killed in a car bombing in Benghazi on Monday night.

According to the LNA, an explosive device attached to al-Mansouri's vehicle detonated as he left a mosque. Authorities have not identified those responsible.

Khaled Haftar, one of Khalifa Haftar's sons, said an investigation had been opened, adding that initial "indicators point to a despicable terrorist tactic," according to AFP news agency.

His office later said authorities had arrested a "terrorist cell" in Benghazi that was allegedly preparing acts of sabotage, but did not say whether it was linked to al-Mansouri's killing.

Al-Mansouri was a prominent military figure close to the Haftar family and had played a key role in fighting jihadist groups in eastern Libya.

How has Libya's political division affected oil production?

The split between dueling administrations has stunted the country's oil producing progress and kept foreign investors wary as rival sides clash over control of the oil revenues that pour into the Central Bank of Libya.

In 2024, a standoff over control of the bank slashed the country's oil exports by more than half.

Libya holds Africa's largest proven oil reserves, yet has struggled to return to pre-2011 production levels of 1.6 million barrels per day. June production hit 1.44 million barrels per day, the highest output levels since 2013, but far short of its target of 2 million barrels per day.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: UNESCO: 2.4 million girls barred from school in Afghanistan
entries.summary: Five years after the Taliban returned to power, millions of Afghan girls remain excluded from secondary education. UNESCO warns of lasting social and economic consequences.
entries.content:
Afghanistan

UNESCO: 2.4 million girls barred from school in Afghanistan

August 12, 2026

Five years after the Taliban returned to power, millions of Afghan girls remain excluded from secondary education. UNESCO warns of lasting social and economic consequences.

Around 2.4 million girls in Afghanistan have been denied access to secondary education since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, UNESCO said Tuesday.

The figure has risen by about 200,000 since last year and could reach nearly four million by 2030 if the ban remains in place.

"Afghanistan remains the only country in the world where girls and women are formally banned from secondary and higher education," Hoda Jaberian, UNESCO’s program coordinator for education in emergencies, said.

"Five years is not a temporary interruption in a child’s education. It is clearly almost an entire secondary school cycle."

Why are Afghan girls banned from secondary schools and universities?

The Taliban seized power on August 15, 2021, as US and NATO forces withdrew after two decades of war.

They initially assured the international community that women would be allowed to continue studying.

But secondary schools were closed to girls in March 2022. Women were barred from universities in December that year.

The Taliban described both measures as temporary, but they remain in force.

The authorities say they respect women's rights in line with their interpretation of Islamic law and Afghan culture. They have also insisted the issue is a domestic matter.

Restrictions extend beyond education. Women face limits on employment and movement and have been barred from public parks, gyms and beauty salons.

The UN has described the broader system of restrictions as “gender apartheid.” Russia is the only country to formally recognize the Taliban administration.

What has happened to girls' education since the Taliban takeover?

UNESCO says the restrictions have reversed two decades of progress.

Girls had very limited access to schooling in 2001. By 2021, nearly one million were enrolled in secondary education.

"Afghanistan had made really major progress in expanding girls’ access to education," Jaberian said. "But unfortunately, much of that progress now has been completely reversed."

UNESCO has called for the immediate and unconditional restoration of girls' and women's right to secondary and higher education.

The agency continues to support community-based education as well as literacy and skills programs, often held in community spaces or facilitators' homes.

How is the Taliban ban affecting Afghanistan's economy?

UNESCO estimates that excluding women from secondary and higher education could push around 600,000 women out of the workforce by 2066.

The restrictions could also cause cumulative income losses of 9.6 billion US dollars and increase the risk of early marriage.

The ban is also worsening a shortage of female teachers. UNESCO expects Afghanistan to face a deficit of more than 11,000 qualified female teachers by 2030.

"Many teachers have left the country and those who were in the system are banned from continuing teaching," Jaberian said.

She added that restrictions on women teaching boys had left some pupils with unqualified male teachers or no teachers at all.

How severe is Afghanistan's wider education crisis?

Afghanistan's education system is facing problems far beyond the ban on girls.

More than two million primary school children are already out of school for other reasons. More than 90% of 10-year-olds cannot read a simple text, while the national literacy rate stands at 37%.

Many schools are overcrowded and poorly equipped. Nearly half lack water, sanitation or heating.

The system is also under pressure from people returning to Afghanistan.

Three million people returned in 2025 alone, either voluntarily or forcibly. More than seven million have returned or been forced back since 2023.

Natural disasters have added to the crisis. Earthquakes, floods and other disasters have forced around 1,000 schools to close since 2021, UNESCO said.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

entries.title: Ebola: Over 2,000 dead in DR Congo as virus gathers pace
entries.summary: Authorities in the DRC say the Ebola virus is killing faster than any outbreak on record. Scientists have also said the outbreak may have started earlier than previously thought.
entries.content:
August 11, 2026

Authorities in the DRC say the Ebola virus is killing faster than any outbreak on record. Scientists have also said the outbreak may have started earlier than previously thought.

Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) said on Tuesday that an outbreak of a particularly virulent strain of the Bundibugyo Ebola virus currently raging in the east and northeast of the country has killed more than 2,000 people since the first case was confirmed.

In all, more than 4,380 infections have been recorded.

The current outbreak is the 17th ever recorded in the DRC, with Sania Nishtar of the Gavi global vaccine alliance warning it could become "the largest outbreak ever."

Until now, the worst outbreak recorded in the DRC was the one that took place from 2018 to 2020 when some 3,500 infections led to 2,300 deaths.

The pace of death is gathering momentum this time around, with the virus spreading faster and exhibiting a higher mortality rate than the 2014-2016 West African outbreak — the worst outbreak on record, which logged 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths.

The current DRC outbreak was declared on May 15, but health authorities say the first transmissions likely took place in February of earlier still.

The 1,000-death mark was not reached until nine weeks in, now — in just three-weeks' time — that figure has doubled again.

The case fatality rate of the current outbreak is 45.9% compared to 39.6% in the 2014-2016 West African outbreak.

'We haven't reached the peak yet,' says DRC health minister

Though there are vaccines against some strains of the Ebola virus, there are currently none approved for the rare Bundibugyo strain that is spreading across the DRC faster than health authorities can trace it.

Moreover, health authorities face massive logistics challenges due to the volatile security situation in the country, where bad roads and rebel violence coupled with lack of healthcare worker pay and mass strikes make it increasingly difficult to keep tabs on the illness.

"We haven't reached the peak yet," said Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba in an interview shared by the ministry on X. "Within the next three months, we expect to have already brought the spread under control and to start seeing it decline," he added.

Ebola, which is transmitted through physical contact with bodily fluids, causing a hemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past half century.

Authorities in the DRC have placed restrictions on public gatherings as well as closing the airport in Ituri Province, the epicenter of the outbreak. Still, fighting and disease have forced the displacement of masses of people in the DRC, Rwanda and South Sudan.

On Monday, the World Health Organization's (WHO) regional director told reporters that authorities are "chasing the virus… the virus is ahead of us."

What's the latest on bids to treat or vaccinate this Ebola strain?

Clinical trials for two antiviral treatment methods have been ongoing since early July and on Friday the WHO recommended undertaking a full-scale human trial of the Ervebo vaccine.

Although Ervebo has proven effective against the Zaire strain of Ebola, its efficacy in fighting the Bundibugyo strain is unproven. WHO officials are hopeful that it can offer some protection against the DRC strain.

Vaccine alliance Gavi says it has made some 500,000 doses of Ervebo in its stockpiles available for the trial.

Virologists say the new Bundibugyo strain appears to have been transmitted from animals to humans and has changed from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012.

Researchers from Congo, Uganda, Belgium and other countries published findings ‌in the journal Nature Medicine on Monday, suggesting the outbreak began ‌with an animal-to-human transmission event and was then spread between people.

Given the severity of the outbreak, authorities are looking into the possibility that the pathogen may have mutated.

Jean Kaseya, the head of the Africa CDC, last week warned that fewer and fewer new cases could be traced back to contacts of existing confirmed patients, with researchers falling well below the WHO's targets of tracking 95% of potential contacts to contain the spread.

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier

entries.title: Ex-Marine released and returning to US from Russian prison
entries.summary: A US citizen and former military serviceman has been released after four years in prison in Russia. President Trump said the release was not part of any exchange and expressed appreciation to Russia's Putin.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Ex-Marine released and returning to US from Russian prison

August 11, 2026

A US citizen and former military serviceman has been released after four years in prison in Russia. President Trump said the release was not part of any exchange and expressed appreciation to Russia's Putin.

Russia on Tuesday released Robert Gilman, a former US Marine who had spent more than four years in prison on disputed charges, according to a group advocating for him and US officials. 

US President Donald Trump and the State Department both said the release was on "humanitarian grounds" and that it was not part of an exchange or prisoner swap with Russia. 

Who is Robert Gilman?

The 32-year-old former service member had been working as a teacher in Russia when he was first detained in 2022, accused of assaulting a police officer after being ejected from a train for causing a disturbance.

He was later accused of other violent offenses while incarcerated and was given a longer jail sentences, ultimately reaching a total of roughly 10 years.

Advocacy group Global Reach had warned of Gilman's deteriorating health condition in detention. His mother was in Russia trying to secure his release as the news developed.

What did Trump and the State Department say about the release?

Trump posted about the release on his Truth Social platform, also including what appeared to be a photo of a sedentary Gilman, his mother and others on a plane, holding an American flag.

"After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis," Trump wrote. "We appreciated the decision, and the fact that Russia asked for no one in return — No exchange took place." 

He said that Gilman and others would land at Andrews Air Force Base in Washington later on Tuesday to be welcomed back to the US.

The State Department, meanwhile, issued a statement attributed to Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

"We thank Russia for working with Special Envoy Steve Witkoff to release Mr. Gilman and allowing him to receive the necessary medical treatment here in the United States," Rubio said. "While we appreciate this positive step, we are still seeking the immediate return of all other unjustly detained Americans, including wrongful detainee Stephen Hubbard."

The statement lauded Trump's efforts to free US-Americans from foreign detention during his second term and concluded that Trump "will not stop until all unjustly detained Americans are home."

Gilman's sister credits Trump, Democrat senator with her brother's release

Gilman's sister Lexie Hudson said in a statement from advocacy group Global Reach that Trump hearing about the case and taking action was the "reason that Robert is alive today."

She also thanked Democrat Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey "for leading our advocacy efforts in Congress."

"The Russians treated my brother so badly," Hudson said. "They hurt him for no reason, other than that he was both an American and a Marine. What did they get out of this? Why did they do this to such a wonderful person?"

According to Global Reach's chief strategy officer Eric Lebson, Gilman had been in a "dissociative stupor" for 47 days, attributing this to abuse he suffered in prison.

He had been moved to a civilian hospital prior to his release, and would soon be medically and psychologically assessed and treated at a US military hospital, Lebson said.

Gilman's mother had traveled to Russia amid the reports of her son's deteriorating health to try to see him.

"It is a tragedy that it took Robert's near-death condition for his case to receive the attention that it required for his release to be negotiated," Massachusetts Senator Markey said in the statement from Global Reach. "Throughout his detention, Robert was subjected to physical torture, forced medication, and provocations by Russian authorities. There is no doubt that his treatment by Russian authorities is the reason Robert is in this precarious state today."

Gilman was arrested in January 2022, a few weeks before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. His prosecution proceeded as relations between Putin's Russia and NATO members deteriorated markedly. 

Edited by: Rebecca Staudenmaier

entries.title: Can Turkey's new PKK law bring peace?
entries.summary: Turkey's parliament has passed a framework law for the peace process with the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK). What does it stipulate, why is it controversial and what does it mean for the future of the peace process?
entries.content:
Turkey

Can Turkey's new PKK law bring peace?

August 11, 2026

Turkey's parliament has passed a framework law for the peace process with the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK). What does it stipulate, why is it controversial and what does it mean for the future of the peace process?

One year ago, the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) burned its weapons in a symbolic ceremony. The move was seen as a sign of its willingness to disband. Since then, the Kurdish side has been calling on the Turkish government to take political steps.

Now, parliament has passed a bill submitted by the conservative Islamic ruling party AKP and its ultranationalist ally. Officially called the "Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration," it is intended to provide the legal framework for the ongoing peace process.

According to official figures, 467 out of 592 MPs voted in favor of the bill. The ruling party and its ally see this as the beginning of a new era: Under certain conditions, the bill provides for a suspension of sentences for PKK members — but only after the PKK and its affiliated groups have been confirmed to have disbanded and disarmed, so that peace, brotherhood and solidarity can prevail throughout the entire country.

The pro-Kurdish DEM party also supports the bill, but it views it only as a first step that must be followed by further reforms.

PKK law divides society and parliament

Fierce opposition came from the ultranationalist opposition party IYI. Even during consultations, its delegate Ayyuce Turkes, daughter of the founder of the ultranationalist and right-wing extremist Grey Wolves, accused the government of rushing a landmark bill through parliament.

She also criticized what she felt was an overly conciliatory stance toward PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan. She avoided using his name, calling him a "baby killer" instead, just as government agencies and media have done for decades. There was even a physical altercation.

The debate highlights just how deep the divides are within Turkish society. While the ultranationalist IYI party rejects the process, the MHP, from which the Grey Wolves emerged, is now among its most important supporters — even though it had, previously, vehemently opposed earlier peace initiatives.

Observers believe this shift in course and the progress in the peace process are also a result of the changed security situation in the region. Among other things, they mention the fall of the Assad regime in Syria, the war in Gaza and the conflict between Israel, the United States and Iran. Syria and Iran are also home to large Kurdish populations that are supported by various regional actors.

According to the prevailing view, a more stable relationship with the Kurds who live within Turkey's own borders could provide Ankara with more leeway in domestic and foreign policy.

What's in the law?

The law applies to convictions for PKK membership, propaganda, financing or intentional support of the organization and its structures. For prison sentences of up to 15 years, enforcement is to be suspended for five years; for longer or life sentences, the suspension is to last ten years. Ongoing investigations are to be put on hold. According to pro-government media, up to 3,600 prisoners could benefit from this.

The prerequisite is the complete disbanding of the PKK and the surrender of all its weapons and ammunition. Both of these conditions have to be verified by Turkish authorities and, subsequently, officially confirmed by the National Security Council, chaired by Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Excluded are PKK members who were convicted prior to June 1, 2005 — the date on which the current penal code came into force — as well as those convicted of homicide and whose convictions are final. That means the regulation does not apply to PKK founder Ocalan either. In February 2025, the 77-year-old had called on the PKK to disband, declared an end to the armed struggle and spoke out in favor of a political solution.

PKK views law as a mere first step

The PKK also calls the bill a first step; it criticizes, however, wording and content. Its key demand remained unfulfilled: As long as Ocalan cannot directly coordinate the peace process under conditions of freedom, the issue of disarmament could not be resolved either.

They said penal code regulations alone did not go far enough, more comprehensive democratization reforms were needed. The message was that as long as returning fighters or exiled politicians continued to be criminalized and were unable to engage in political activities legally, hardly any of them would leave the mountains where they've been staying.

Even legal pro-Kurdish political activity has ben restricted in Turkey for decades: parties were banned, politicians were arrested or barred from political activity. To this day, elected mayors are being removed from office, and numerous politicians and activists are in prison. Among them are two former co-chairs of the Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP) that mainly represented Kurds, Selahattin Demirtas and Figen Yuksekdag.

Peace without democratization?

Political scientist Berk Esen criticizes the law for failing to offer concrete democratic solutions to the Kurdish issue. He also noted that, parallel to the peace process involving the PKK, the government had significantly increased the pressure on the largest opposition party CHP.

For about two years, the Turkish judiciary has increasingly been cracking down on leading CHP politicians. Critics view this as an attempt to weaken the government party's strongest political rival. Among the most high-profile cases is that of former mayor of Istanbul and CHP presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu. He and hundreds of other party members are in prison, on charges of fraud and corruption.

The entire CHP leadership under Ozgur Ozel was removed as well. He formed a new party several weeks ago.

Criticism of Erdogan's role

Esen primarily criticizes Erdogan's strong influence on the peace process. Although it is to be implemented by a committee chaired by the vice president and key ministers, who are also heads of the intelligence services and the National Security Council, Esen argues that it will ultimately be Erdogan as chairman of the National Security Council who decides when and which steps in the peace process will be implemented.

This assessment is also shared by Reha Ruhavioglu, director of the Kurdish Studies Center.

"Erdogan will clearly set the pace," Ruhavioglu said, attributing this to the asymmetric balance of power between the Turkish state and the PKK.

In addition, Erdogan had learned his lessons from the failure of the peace talks between 2013 and 2015 and would now certainly assemble more control in his own hands. At the same time, experts say, Erdogan has his sights set firmly on the 2028 presidential and parliamentary elections, and would want to limit any political risks associated with the process.

Ruhavioglu expects further controversy, especially if former PKK fighters return to Turkey and remain at large. The government is therefore likely to allow their return, suspended sentences and political activity only gradually, and largely in response to public reaction.
